job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Emeka Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I run for forty minutes along the canal, then I'm at the laptop by nine. I tweak my CV for whichever bank or building society I'm targeting, and I usually do one online test a day. I share a rented house in Birmingham with my friend Kofi, who's a trainee teacher, and in the afternoons I do shifts of volunteer money advice at a community centre. I finished economics and finance at Warwick in the summer with a first, and I've had no offer yet, which still stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I never believed the hype anyway. At the community centre I'd say people will still need a person to explain a loan to them. Online I'd say nothing, honestly, I'm not a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel quite calm. There are plenty of finance jobs round here, and my internship at the credit union taught me that most of the work is talking to members, not running software. My only private worry is that I want my first proper job now, not in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Four applications a week, aimed carefully, and I'd keep the money advice shifts since they're on my CV. I'd ask my old boss at the credit union, Mrs Adeyemi, whether the lending team is recruiting. I'd also put a bit more into my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. I don't feel sick about it. I feel like a man waiting for a bus that he knows is coming, just late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents. My mum is a teacher and my dad dispatches taxis, and they paid for a lot of my life up to now. I want to be able to say I pay my own way, even though they'd never ask me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, mainly, and Mrs Adeyemi. Kofi says I overthink. Mrs Adeyemi says to keep the volunteer work going because lenders like people who've sat with real borrowers. Both of them are right, I think.

say: I'd say people will still need a **real person** to explain a loan.
I'd say little online; I'm **not a poster**.
think: The credit union taught me most of the job is **talking to members**.
I just want my first **proper job** sooner, not in March.
do: Send about **four careful applications** a week and keep the money advice shifts.
Ask Mrs Adeyemi whether the **lending team** is hiring.
feel: **Steady**, like waiting for a bus that is coming, just late.
S0.quote: I feel like a man waiting for a bus that he knows is coming, just late.
fieldNote: Calm comes from **plenty of local openings** and a strong cushion.
Wants to pay his own way, a pressure from his parents' sacrifices.
Values human contact in finance, which shapes his optimism.

steps.text: Send four targeted applications a week to banks and building societies
Ask Mrs Adeyemi if the credit union lending team is hiring
Move another chunk of savings into his emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, but it's not the end of the world. At the community centre I'd say we need to check that firms still train people, not just hire experts. If my union had a graduate section I'd be in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means fewer junior jobs and more pressure to show I'm worth hiring. The checking and reporting I did at the bank internship would go to software first. I think I'd still get a job, but a narrower one, and probably a lower one than I expect now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools properly for my own work, like summarising reports and building spreadsheets. I'd apply wider, to compliance, lending, advice and public-sector roles, because those need people to sign things off. I'd also join the finance workers' union as soon as I had a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I'm not scared of losing the thing I don't have yet, but I'm aware I could end up as the person who got the last easy-ish graduate job instead of the first of a bigger wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Churning out reports, checking invoices, building first drafts of credit memos. I did a lot of exactly that at the bank. I'd tell a friend who graduates next year to learn the tools now, and to get used to talking to customers as soon as they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get one specialism, like lending to small firms, and stay close to the people who sign off on risk. And don't wait for firms to teach you the tools. I learned mine from videos at 11pm, and I'd do the same again.

say: I'd say firms must keep **training people**, not only hire experts.
I'd join a **graduate union** section if there was one.
think: Software takes the **checking and reporting** I did first, so fewer junior jobs.
I'll likely get a **narrower job** than I now expect.
do: Learn **AI tools** properly, starting with report summaries and spreadsheet models.
Apply wider to **compliance, lending, advice** and public-sector roles that need sign-off.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, not scared of losing what I don't have yet.
S1.quote: I'd tell a friend who graduates next year to learn the tools now, and to get used to talking to customers as soon as they can.
fieldNote: Expects **fewer junior roles** but still believes he'll land one.
Uses AI sometimes now; this scenario pushes him to learn it properly.
Sees human sign-off and customer contact as the safe spots.

steps.text: Learn AI tools for report summaries and spreadsheet models
Apply to compliance, lending and advice roles as well
Join the finance workers' union once he has a job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something dramatic, honestly. That it's moving faster than any government or firm can handle, and everyone should be told the truth. At work, if I had work, I'd be asking what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. If the thing can do the thinking work of a graduate, cheaper, the firms I'm applying to won't be hiring, and a first-class degree won't make a difference. I'd be worried about my parents' savings too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd check what I have. I have over six months saved, and my parents would help. I'd get a safe job, any job, even a retail or care one, to have income. And I'd go to my MP's surgery with other graduates and make a noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Two years is hardly time to finish a training course. I'd go to bed worried and wake up still thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next months stop being about the perfect first job. They're about income and about who will help. I'd talk to the council about retraining places and I'd ask Kofi whether his school needs a teaching assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my mum and dad that I'm okay for now, I've got a cushion, and we face it as a family. I'd also say sorry, because they put a lot into my degree and I'd feel it was wasted.

say: I'd say it's moving **faster than anyone** can handle and we should be told the truth.
I'd ask my employer, if I had one, **what the plan is**.
think: If the machine does graduate-level thinking cheaper, firms **stop hiring**, and my first-class degree won't help.
I'd worry about my **parents' savings** too.
do: Take **any steady job**, even in retail or care, for income.
Go to my MP's surgery with **other graduates**.
feel: **Anxious**: two years is hardly time to finish a training course.
S2.quote: Two years is hardly time to finish a training course.
fieldNote: Savings and family backing keep him at **anxious**, not alarmed.
Shifts from the perfect first job to **any income** and collective pressure.
Feels guilty that his parents' investment in his degree might be wasted.

steps.text: Take any steady job, even retail or care, to bring in income
Go to the MP's surgery with other graduates to demand support
Ask the council about retraining places
Tell his parents his savings can cover six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real warning and it shouldn't be wasted. I'd say the useful question is what we do with the time. I'd probably write to my MP and my old tutors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get a job, probably a good one, and I'd have to treat it as a launchpad. I'd also be thinking about what a normal career means when a machine does the thinking. I'd rather be a person who helps people with money than a person who builds spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best offer and ask them to put me in the customer-facing team. I'd learn AI tools as part of the job and save around a third of my pay. By year two I'd have started a part-time diploma in financial advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a good job on the horizon with a cloud over it. It isn't panic. I feel like someone who knows a storm is coming and has time to buy a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd scramble. With five, I'd plan. I'd build the diploma and the savings in order, rather than at once, and I'd try to buy a flat share with Kofi's cousin so my rent stays low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop being picky about the first job being perfect. And I'd start paying attention to which firms treat their juniors well, because those firms will survive the change better.

say: I'd say five years is a **real warning** and we shouldn't waste it.
I'd **write to my MP** and my old tutors.
think: I'll get a job, and I should treat it as a **launchpad**.
I'd rather **help people with money** than build spreadsheets.
do: Take the best offer and ask for the **customer-facing** team.
Start a part-time **financial advice** diploma by year two.
feel: **Uneasy**: like knowing a storm is coming and having time to buy a coat.
S3.quote: I feel like someone who knows a storm is coming and has time to buy a coat.
fieldNote: Time lets him **plan in order**: job, savings, then a diploma.
Wants to move towards **advice work**, which needs people.
Names a concrete saving of about a third of his pay.

steps.text: Take the best offer and ask to join the customer-facing team
Save about a third of each month's pay
Start a part-time financial advice diploma in year two
Use AI tools at work from the first week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it on arguing. At home I'd say the sensible thing is to start preparing schools and training now. I'd probably volunteer for a local group that teaches adults the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly okay. A whole decade is a career, or the start of one. I'd still be aware that the finance job I'm training for might not exist at 33, so I'd keep one eye on the exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the job, work hard, and take the advice diploma and then maybe a master's part-time. I'd save and buy a flat by about 28, which I'd have wanted anyway. I'd also volunteer teaching people to use the new tools at the community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd have time to find my way, and I'd have savings by then. I'm 23 and finding it hard to be scared of something ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a mild plan in place and not stress. If I'm in my early thirties when it lands, I'll be an experienced person with a cushion. The risk is that I get complacent, and I'd have to watch for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, slightly. A decade feels safe, but the point of having ten years is that I could make changes, and I know I'm the sort who waits. So I'd try to set a check-in every year to see where things are.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and we shouldn't waste it arguing.
I'd back local **training** for schools and adults now.
think: A decade is a **career**, but my finance job may not exist at 33.
I'd keep **one eye** on the exit.
do: Work hard, finish a **diploma**, and maybe a part-time master's.
Teach adults at the community centre to use the **new tools**.
feel: Mostly **calm**: it's hard to fear something ten years away at 23.
S4.quote: I'm 23 and finding it hard to be scared of something ten years away.
fieldNote: The decade makes him **calm**, though he knows he tends to wait.
Wants a yearly check-in so complacency doesn't creep in.
Links ten years of notice to community teaching and a flat by 28.

steps.text: Finish the advice diploma and then a part-time master's
Buy a flat by 28 using a steady monthly saving
Teach adults to use the new tools at the community centre

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the one where my cushion and my degree don't count for much, because nobody has time to adjust. What would help is clear information early, a guaranteed place on a retraining scheme, and employers being open about what they plan. I'd also like to see some kind of basic support for people stuck between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more relaxed than I sound, and that's partly luck. I have savings and a family who'd catch me. I'd like to think about the graduates who don't.

headlineQuote: I have savings and a family who'd catch me. I'd like to think about the graduates who don't.
portrait: Emeka is 23, a **top graduate** in economics and finance from Warwick, sharing a rented house in Birmingham.
He does volunteer money advice and values **human contact** in finance work.
He uses AI tools now and then and learns them when others have proved them.
His mood runs from **calm** to anxious, and the 2028 world is the only one that truly frightens him.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, where his degree and cushion matter little.
whatWouldHelp: **Early information**, a guaranteed retraining place, and open employers.
